ed.title: Yesterday words
ed.say: Some words tell us about things that already happened. They wear two little letters at the end: e, d. Lived, loved, played, gathered, thanked. All of these are over and done.
ed.spoken: Yesterday words. Some words tell us about things that already happened. They wear two little letters at the end: E and D. Lived, loved, played, gathered, and thanked. All of these are over and done.

marks.title: Asking or telling?
marks.say: Every sentence ends with a little mark. When Badal asks Maa something, the sentence ends with a question mark. When Maa tells him something, it ends with a full stop.
marks.spoken: Asking or telling? Every sentence ends with a little mark. When Badal asks Maa something, the sentence ends with a question mark. When Maa tells him something, it ends with a full stop.

pairs.title: Best-friend words
pairs.say: Badal and Moti go everywhere together. Some words are best friends too, like paper and pencil. We join them with the little word: and.
pairs.spoken: Best-friend words. Badal and Moti go everywhere together. Some words are best friends too, like paper and pencil. We join them with the little word, and.

recall.title: Show what you know
recall.say: Answer these on your own, no looking back! Yesterday words, end marks, best-friend words, and the story of Badal and Moti.
recall.spoken: Show what you know. Answer these on your own, with no looking back! Yesterday words, end marks, best-friend words, and the story of Badal and Moti.

ed.text: Meet Badal and his puppy Moti! Today, Moti PLAYS in the garden with Badal.
ed.spoken: Meet Badal and his puppy Moti! Today, Moti plays in the garden with Badal.

ed.text: Now think about YESTERDAY. The sun has gone down, the moon is up. Moti played then too — but that is already over. It is finished!
ed.spoken: Now think about yesterday. The sun has gone down, and the moon is up. Moti played then too, but that is already over. It is finished!

ed.text: To show an action already happened, we add two little letters to the end of the word. Here they come: e and d!
ed.spoken: To show that an action already happened, we add two little letters to the end of the word. Here they come: E, and D!

ed.text: play plus e-d makes played. Yesterday, Moti PLAYED with Badal.
ed.spoken: Play, plus E D, makes played. Yesterday, Moti played with Badal.

ed.text: The story is full of -ed words: lived, loved, played, gathered, thanked. Every one of them already happened!
ed.spoken: The story is full of E D words: lived, loved, played, gathered, and thanked. Every one of them already happened!

marks.text: One rainy evening, Badal found a little puppy shivering in the cold. He took him home. Now he wants to ASK Maa something.
marks.spoken: One rainy evening, Badal found a little puppy shivering in the cold. He took him home. Now he wants to ask Maa something.

marks.text: “Can this puppy stay with us, Maa” — Badal is asking. An asking sentence is a QUESTION.
marks.spoken: Can this puppy stay with us, Maa? Badal is asking. An asking sentence is a question.

marks.text: A question ends with a question mark. Watch it hop in!
marks.spoken: A question ends with a question mark. Watch it hop in!

marks.text: Maa answers: “Yes beta, but only if you promise to take care of the puppy” — Maa is TELLING, not asking.
marks.spoken: Maa answers, Yes, beta, but only if you promise to take care of the puppy. Maa is telling, not asking.

marks.text: A telling sentence ends with a full stop. Here it comes!
marks.spoken: A telling sentence ends with a full stop. Here it comes!

marks.text: Asking words often start a question: What, Where, Who, Whose, Can, May. Telling sentences just tell.
marks.spoken: Asking words often start a question: What, Where, Who, Whose, Can, and May. Telling sentences just tell.

pairs.text: Badal and Moti are best friends. They go everywhere together!
pairs.spoken: Badal and Moti are best friends. They go everywhere together!

pairs.text: Some WORDS are best friends too. Think of a bat. What does it need?
pairs.spoken: Some words are best friends too. Think of a bat. What does it need?

pairs.text: A ball! Here it comes rolling. We join best-friend words with the little word “and”: bat and ball.
pairs.spoken: A ball! Here it comes rolling. We join best-friend words with the little word, and: bat and ball.

pairs.text: A lock is no use without its key: lock and key. And idli tastes best with sambar: idli and sambar!
pairs.spoken: A lock is no use without its key: lock and key. And idli tastes best with sambar: idli and sambar!

pairs.text: Now you find the pairs. Tap a word on the left, then tap its best friend on the right.
pairs.spoken: Now you find the pairs. Tap a word on the left, then tap its best friend on the right.

prompt-ed.spoken: Read each sentence. Is the action already over, or happening now? Pick the word that fits. When -ed is needed, watch the machine stamp it on!

prompt-marks.spoken: These six sentences are from your book. Say each one out loud. Is it asking or telling? Post the right mark on the end.

prompt-pairs.spoken: Tap a word on the left, then tap its best friend on the right. A matched pair gets its own colour, just like in your book.

machine-walk.spoken: Yesterday, Badal blank, to school. Is it walk, or walked?

machine-play.spoken: Today, Badal and Moti blank, in the garden. Is it play, or played?

machine-talk.spoken: Last night, Maa blank, to Badal about the puppy. Is it talk, or talked?

machine-ask.spoken: Yesterday, Badal blank, Maa a question. Is it ask, or asked?

machine-touch.spoken: Yesterday, Badal gently blank, the wet puppy. Is it touch, or touched?

post-sun.spoken: The sun rises in the east

post-borrow.spoken: May I borrow your English textbook

post-friends.spoken: Brinda and Namrata are good friends

q-ed-book-walk.spoken: Add ed and write: walk + ed = ? Your choices are: walked, or walking, or walks, or walkes.

q-ed-fresh-already.spoken: Which word tells us the action ALREADY happened? Your choices are: jump, or jumped, or jumps, or jumping.

q-ed-fresh-follow.spoken: Yesterday, Moti blank Badal's scent and found him. Which word fits? Your choices are: follow, or followed, or follows.

q-marks-fresh-question.spoken: Which of these is a QUESTION? Your choices are: Moti is a brown puppy, or Where does Moti sleep, or Badal loves Moti, or The pit was deep.

q-marks-fresh-who.spoken: Pick the end mark: Who pulled Badal out of the pit blank Your choices are: a question mark, or a full stop.

q-marks-book-mangoes.spoken: Add a ? or a . — I like to eat mangoes blank Your choices are: a full stop, or a question mark.

q-pairs-book-needle.spoken: Match the pair: needle and blank Your choices are: thread, or table, or ball, or key.

q-pairs-fresh-which.spoken: Which pair goes together? Your choices are: chair and sambar, or bat and ball, or lock and pencil.

q-pairs-fresh-badal.spoken: Complete the best-friend pair from the story: Badal and blank Your choices are: Moti, or the pit, or the rope.

q-recall-ed-lived.spoken: Which word tells about something that already happened? Your choices are: live, or lived, or living.

q-recall-ed-pulled.spoken: Yesterday, the neighbours blank Badal out of the pit. Your choices are: pull, or pulled, or pulls.

q-recall-marks-whose.spoken: Pick the end mark: Whose puppy is this blank Your choices are: a question mark, or a full stop.

q-recall-marks-gate.spoken: Pick the end mark: Moti waited at the gate blank Your choices are: a full stop, or a question mark.

q-recall-pairs-idli.spoken: Which pair is right? Your choices are: idli and sambar, or idli and key, or idli and thread.

q-recall-story-first.spoken: What happened FIRST in the story? Your choices are: Badal fell into a deep pit, or Badal came across a puppy by the side of the road, or Moti went near the pit and barked.

m-is-it-happening-now.spoken: Is it happening now?. Try a smaller one: “Today, Moti JUMP for joy.” Today means it is happening right now, not finished — so no -ed. We say jump. Remember: -ed is only for actions that are already over.

m-look-for-the-time-word-first.spoken: Look for the time word first. Try a smaller one: “Yesterday, Moti WAIT at the gate.” Yesterday is over, so the waiting already happened — we say waited. Remember: If the action already happened, the word wears its -ed.

m-just-add-the-two-letters.spoken: Just add the two letters. Take a smaller word: jump. Put e and d on the end and nothing else changes: jump + ed = jumped. Remember: Add e-d to the end of the word. Do not change the rest.

m-look-at-the-last-two-letters.spoken: Look at the last two letters. Compare cook and cooked. Only cooked ends in -ed, so only cooked is already over — like the food Maa cooked yesterday. Remember: The word ending in -ed is the one that already happened.

m-yesterday-is-over.spoken: Yesterday is over. Try: “Yesterday, Moti BARK at the pit.” Yesterday is finished, so the barking already happened: barked. Remember: Yesterday, last night, last week → the word needs -ed.

m-this-one-wants-an-answer.spoken: This one wants an answer. Try a smaller sentence: “Where is Moti” — it is asking, it needs someone to answer. So it ends with a question mark: Where is Moti? Remember: An asking sentence ends with a question mark.

m-this-one-is-only-telling.spoken: This one is only telling. Try a smaller sentence: “Moti is a puppy” — nobody is asking anything, it just tells us. So it ends with a full stop: Moti is a puppy. Remember: A telling sentence ends with a full stop.

m-listen-for-the-asking-word.spoken: Listen for the asking word. Compare “The rope is long” with “How long is the rope”. Only the second one wants an answer, and it starts with an asking word: How. Remember: A question wants an answer and often starts with an asking word.

m-who-is-an-asking-word.spoken: Who is an asking word. Try: “Who is barking” — it wants a name as an answer, so it is asking: Who is barking? Remember: Sentences that begin with Who, What, Where or Whose are questions.

m-nobody-is-asking-here.spoken: Nobody is asking here. Try: “Moti likes bones” — it simply tells us something Moti likes. No answer is needed, so it ends with a full stop. Remember: A sentence that tells ends with a full stop.

m-ask-what-it-is-used-with.spoken: Ask what it is used with. Try a smaller pair: salt and … pepper! Salt and pepper sit together on every table. Ask yourself what your left word is always used with. Remember: Best-friend words are the ones we use together.

m-what-does-it-work-with.spoken: What does it work with?. Think of a smaller pair: brush and … paint! A brush needs paint to work. Ask what a needle needs to sew. Remember: A pair is two things that work together.

m-picture-the-two-things-together.spoken: Picture the two things together. Picture “shoes and socks”. You can see them together. Now picture “shoes and sambar” — that does not fit! Only real pairs make a picture. Remember: A real pair is easy to picture together.

m-who-is-always-together.spoken: Who is always together?. In the story, one friend followed Badal wherever he went, ate with him and played with him. That friend is his pair. Remember: Best friends make the best pairs.

m-look-for-the-ed.spoken: Look for the -ed. Compare hop and hopped. Only hopped ends in -ed, so only hopped is already over. Remember: -ed at the end means it already happened.

m-yesterday-is-over-2.spoken: Yesterday is over. Try: “Yesterday, Moti WAIT at the gate.” Yesterday is finished, so it is waited. Remember: Already happened → add -ed.

m-whose-is-an-asking-word.spoken: Whose is an asking word. Try: “Whose bag is that” — it wants a name as an answer, so it is asking: Whose bag is that? Remember: Asking sentences end with a question mark.

m-this-one-only-tells.spoken: This one only tells. Try: “The rope was strong” — nobody is asking, it just tells. So it ends with a full stop. Remember: Telling sentences end with a full stop.

m-think-of-your-plate.spoken: Think of your plate. Picture “bread and butter” — you eat them together. Ask what you eat idli with. Remember: Pairs are things used together.

m-start-at-the-very-beginning.spoken: Start at the very beginning. Think of a smaller story: first you find a seed, then you plant it, then it grows. Badal had to MEET Moti before Moti could help him. Remember: Ask: what had to happen before anything else could?

sol-ed-book-walk.spoken: Why this works. Start with walk. Add e and d to the end. walk + ed = walked. Remember: Add -ed to show the action already happened.

sol-ed-fresh-already.spoken: Why this works. Look at the end of each word. Only one word ends in -ed. jumped is the yesterday word. Remember: -ed at the end means already happened.

sol-ed-fresh-follow.spoken: Why this works. The sentence says Yesterday. So the action is already over. follow + ed = followed. Remember: Already happened → add -ed.

sol-marks-fresh-question.spoken: Why this works. Read each sentence. Only one wants an answer. Where does Moti sleep? starts with Where — it asks. Remember: Asking sentences are questions.

sol-marks-fresh-who.spoken: Why this works. The sentence starts with Who. It wants an answer: the neighbours! So it ends with ? Remember: Asking → question mark.

sol-marks-book-mangoes.spoken: Why this works. The sentence tells what I like. It does not want an answer. So it ends with a full stop. Remember: Telling → full stop.

sol-pairs-book-needle.spoken: Why this works. A needle is used for sewing. Thread goes through the needle. needle and thread. Remember: Best-friend words work together.

sol-pairs-fresh-which.spoken: Why this works. Picture each pair. A bat and a ball are used together in a game. bat and ball. Remember: Pairs are things used together.

sol-pairs-fresh-badal.spoken: Why this works. Badal's best friend is his puppy. They ate, played and went everywhere together. Badal and Moti. Remember: and joins two friends.

hint-3-2.spoken: Three small rules. Over → -ed. Asking → ?. Telling → . . Best friends → and.

hint-3-1.spoken: Yesterday, Badal thanked Moti. Yesterday means it already happened, so thank became thanked. A telling sentence, so it ends with a full stop. For example: thank + ed = thanked ..

hint-3-0.spoken: Which rule is it?. Is the question about -ed, about ? and ., or about word pairs?

hint-2-2.spoken: Join the pair with and. Two best-friend words are joined by the little word and.

hint-2-1.spoken: Salt and …. Salt is nearly always with pepper on the table. So the pair is salt and pepper. For example: salt and pepper.

hint-2-0.spoken: Ask what it is used with. Pick a word on the left. What do you always use it with?

hint-1-2.spoken: Ask → ? · Tell → .. Asking sentences end with a question mark. Telling sentences end with a full stop.

hint-1-1.spoken: Where is my bag. This sentence wants an answer, so it is a question. It ends with a question mark. For example: Where is my bag?.

hint-1-0.spoken: Does it want an answer?. If the sentence needs someone to answer it, it is asking.

hint-0-2.spoken: Already happened? Add -ed. If the action is over, add -ed. If it is happening now, leave the word alone.

hint-0-1.spoken: Yesterday, Moti waited. Yesterday is finished. So the waiting already happened, and the word becomes wait + ed. For example: wait + ed = waited.

hint-0-0.spoken: Look for Yesterday or Today. Read the sentence again. Does it say yesterday, last night, or today?
